Research – a systematic inquiry or investigation into a topic – is conducted across the curricula at the University at Albany. Whether it is using ancient texts or more recent diaries to develop new understandings or analyzing data to find mathematical patterns, research is an important component of your university education. Research begins with a question. What answer will you uncover?
Languages, Literatures & Cultures
What is Languages Research?
Linguistics: learn more about the structure of a specific language, its history, variation in how it is used today, and ways to teach and learn it
Literatures: study aspects of human experience explored in literary works and learn to interpret them critically
Cultures: learn more about different cultures and study ways to characterize and teach them and to make global connections
How can I do research in languages at UAlbany?
- Work with faculty on an on-going project
- Carry out research as part of an advanced course
For example, in a course on «Franco-American French », students used Professor Cynthia Fox’s corpus of sociolinguistic interviews to conduct original research on the lexicon of Franco-American French.

Taquile is an island in the middle of Lake Titicaca, a couple hour boat ride from Puno. The Quechua speaking island, though frequently visited by tourists, still retains a very traditional lifestyle, which includes weaving, traditional food and dress, and mythology. The beautifully illustrated book, Kusikiy: A Child From Taquile, Peru by Mercedes Cecilia, offers spectacular insight into the ancient culture still living on this fascinating island.
Children’s books have a way of simplifying unfamiliar ideas and ways of life. Through the story of the young boy Kusikiy, we learn how the islanders of Taquile live. In the tale, Kusikiy learns from his great-grandfather that a constellation is missing from the sky. He asks the APU, the spirit for the glaciers for help, and an adventure ensues that walks us through an array of traditions. We learn the importance of the giant frogs, condors, and flamingos found around and in the high altitude lake. We learn about the stone terraces that continue to decorate the island. claim.title: Colorado-specific named-entity and jurisdiction detector
claim.lede: The neuron is best read as a strongly Colorado-specific feature: it fires on explicit Colorado and Colorado-linked names, institutions, statutes, area codes, URLs, local media and Colorado state-history facts, often at nearby function words, spaces or digits rather than only on the token 'Colorado' itself. The negative pole is contrastive and format-sensitive: comparable administrative, numeric or geographic strings tied to other states/regions, especially Alaska, Dakota, Nevada, Utah, Qinghai and North Dakota, are suppressed. It is not a generic place-name, number, phone or legal-citation detector, because Colorado versions are positive while analogous non-Colorado versions are often negative.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would revise this account if many explicit Colorado mentions, Colorado statutes, 303/720/970 contacts, Colorado university names or Colorado local-news frames gave weak or negative responses without a clear intervening factor. I would also revise it if generic non-Colorado phone numbers, statutes, addresses, area measurements or other state names frequently gave strong positive responses, or if the apparent suppression were better explained by number/punctuation formatting independent of jurisdiction. Finding that the positive pole generalizes to many U.S. state names rather than being dominated by Colorado would weaken the Colorado-specific claim; finding that the strongest negative anchors remain negative even when Colorado context is added would support a separate non-Colorado-identifier or numeric-format feature.
claim.one_paragraph: Strongest positive responses occur in contexts containing 'Colorado' or names built from it: 'state of Colorado', 'University of Colorado', 'Colorado State University', 'Colorado School of Public Health', 'Colorado Department of ...', 'Colorado Women's Education Foundation', 'Colorado Labor Wars', and Colorado places/institutions such as Denver, Boulder, Arvada, Longmont, Aspen, Pueblo and Rocky Mountain. The high value may sit on a nearby function word or space, e.g. 'Its nickname is ...' after a Colorado statehood passage, 'A teacher at ...' after 'a Colorado high school', or 'Atmospheric' inside 'University of Colorado, Boulder, professor emeritus of Atmospheric Science'. Similar names for Alaska, Nevada, Utah, North Dakota or Qinghai do not match and often produce negative activation. A distinct strong pattern is the Colorado Revised Statutes citation structure seen in '§ 22-5-119, C.R.S.', '22-5-199, C.R.S.' and 'per statutory reference in [number]'. High values occur on the spaces, digits or punctuation inside or immediately before these citations in the Colorado blended-learning document. This is not a generic legal/number pattern: an N.D.C.C. § 28-33-02 citation in a North Dakota legal text is strongly negative, and a grant number in a Qinghai math paper is negative. Positive responses also occur on contact/locale strings when the surrounding frame is Colorado: Denver-area 303/720/970 telephone numbers such as 720-848-18..., Colorado ZIP/address forms such as 'Longmont, CO', '.co.us' or 'colostate.edu' URLs, and local media such as 9NEWS. Matches include the high space before 9NEWS, the high slash in the colostate.edu reference URL, and the high space before a Denver-area clinic number after University of Colorado material. Analogous phone/fax strings with 701, 775 or 435 in North Dakota, Nevada or Utah are negative or weak, so the cue is the Colorado frame, not the phone format itself. Colorado state-history frames also produce high activation before or within the relevant fact: 'Colorado became the thirty-eighth state', 'Its nickname is the Centennial State', 'Colorado became a state on August 1, 1876', and 'Colorado Labor Wars, 1903-1904'. The high token can be 'is' before the nickname or a space before the date. Parallel statehood or history facts for other states do not trigger the same positive response unless Colorado is also present; they often sit in weak or negative contexts. Recurring high responses occur around Colorado universities and research/local-news frames: CU Boulder, Colorado State University, University of Colorado, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, NOAA/NCAR in Boulder, Colorado State University Extension, Colorado School of Public Health, and local outlets such as 9NEWS. High values can appear on generic-looking tokens such as 'University', 'State', 'Public', 'Atmospheric', 'Boulder', 'Denver' or nearby spaces/digits. The same generic tokens outside a Colorado-linked name or story do not reliably match; this is why the pattern should be stated as the Colorado named-entity frame rather than as simple keyword membership.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative tokens and examples are dominated by other state, provincial or regional names: Alaska, Dakota, Nevada, Utah, Tahoe, Mojave, Qinghai, Loktak, Zion and similar non-Colorado places. Examples include negative activation on 'Natural' in 'Alaska Natural Heritage Program', on a space before an area figure in a Qinghai article, on a comma in a Nevada 'Wheeler Peak' measurement, and on contact strings in Utah/Nevada material. This appears contrastive: explicit Colorado frames are positive, whereas comparable other-place frames are weak or negative. The strongest negative punctuation/digit anchors often belong to contact, citation or grant strings from other jurisdictions: '(701) 328-1504' in a North Dakota IPM address, a space before a 701 phone number in a North Dakota CWD article, '-' in N.D.C.C. § 28-33-02, '(' in grant No.11761056 from a Qinghai paper, and 775/435 phone strings in Nevada/Utah contexts. This does not mean all numbers are negative; Colorado 720/303 numbers, C.R.S. citations, Longmont CO and colostate.edu are positive. The negative pattern is non-Colorado administrative/contact identifier, not numeric punctuation in general. Negative activation also occurs on digits, commas or hyphens in measurements of non-Colorado places: '278,400 square miles (721,100 square kilometers)' for Qinghai, '13,063-foot Wheeler Peak' in Nevada, and similar area/elevation/date strings in non-Colorado geographic descriptions. This overlaps with the non-Colorado place-name explanation. Generic math or ordinary number strings without a geographic frame are usually weak, and Colorado measurements or Colorado state facts can be positive. Other-jurisdiction administrative and legal boilerplate is negative, especially when it contains addresses, phone/fax numbers, statutory citations or agency names: North Dakota Department of Agriculture/IPM phone block, North Dakota Game and Fish CWD contact, N.D.C.C. citations, and New Mexico or Qinghai grant/address material. The key contrast is that Colorado statutory/contact material is positive even when it has the same format. Matching examples with purely generic legal prose and no other-place or Colorado marker are weaker and sometimes near zero, so the response needs the jurisdiction cue or surrounding context. A narrower negative pattern appears on place-name-like components that resemble Colorado-associated words but lack the Colorado-specific form: singular 'Spring' vs positive 'Springs' (e.g. Colorado Springs), 'Natural' in Alaska Natural Heritage Program, 'Wild' in generic contexts, and names such as Cascade, Fargo, Granite or Sunshine. These are weaker and less consistent than the full place/contact patterns. They support the view that the neuron is tuned to Colorado-specific named entities rather than to the bare words 'state', 'natural', 'spring', 'wild', 'rocky' or 'mountain'.

output.title: Colorado named-entity/jurisdiction frame with narrow other-jurisdiction administrative suppression
output.lede: The neuron is primarily a Colorado named-entity and jurisdiction detector. Strong positives occur on explicit Colorado or Colorado-derived names, Colorado institutions/places, C.R.S. citations, Colorado area codes/URLs/local media, and Colorado statehood/history or higher-education/science frames, often on a nearby space or function word in the causal prefix. The negative pole is much narrower than earlier: broad non-Colorado place-name and measurement rules were withdrawn because many such contexts are positive or weak. Reliable negatives are other-jurisdiction administrative/contact/citation strings; negative coverage is sparse.

positive.name: Explicit Colorado and Colorado-derived named entities in the causal prefix
positive.description: Positive when the prefix before the marked position contains 'Colorado' or a Colorado-built name ('state of Colorado', 'University of Colorado', 'Colorado State University', 'Colorado School of Public Health', 'Colorado Department of ...', 'Colorado Women's Education Foundation', 'Colorado Labor Wars') or a Colorado-linked place/institution ('Denver', 'Boulder', 'Arvada', 'Longmont', 'Aspen', 'Pueblo', 'Rocky Mountain' in a Colorado frame). The high value may sit on an adjacent space or function word inside that name. The cue must be in the causal prefix; continuation after the anchor (e.g. 'Colorado Plateaus' after 'within') does not count. Non-Colorado names do not by themselves establish a negative response.

positive.name: Colorado Revised Statutes citation frame
positive.description: Positive on the Colorado statutory citation pattern '§ 22-5-119, C.R.S.', '22-5-199, C.R.S.' or 'per statutory reference in [number]' within Colorado blended-learning or state-law material. High values can fall on spaces, digits, section symbols, hyphens, or punctuation inside or immediately before the citation. The same punctuation and digits without the Colorado statute frame do not suffice; N.D.C.C. or Qinghai grant numbers are not positive by format alone.

positive.name: Colorado contact, area-code, URL and local-media frames
positive.description: Positive when a Colorado entity/address/local-media frame is present: Denver 303/720/970 numbers such as 720-848-18..., 'Longmont, CO', '.co.us', 'colostate.edu', or '9NEWS'. The high value may be on the space, slash, digit, or adjacent ordinary token. Area code, phone punctuation, or URL form alone is not a cue; analogous 701/775/435 strings in other-jurisdiction administrative material are not positive.

positive.name: Colorado statehood, nickname and historical-event contexts
positive.description: Positive in Colorado state-history frames: 'Colorado became the thirty-eighth state', 'Its nickname is the Centennial State', 'Colorado became a state on August 1, 1876', and 'Colorado Labor Wars, 1903-1904'. The response can land on 'is' before the nickname or a space before the date. Parallel statehood or history facts for other states are not enough; they are not negative by topic alone.

positive.name: Colorado higher-education, science and local-news named-entity frames
positive.description: Positive around Colorado-linked universities, research, and local news: CU Boulder, University of Colorado, Colorado State University, Colorado School of Public Health, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, NOAA/NCAR in Boulder, CSU Extension, and 9NEWS. High values can appear on 'University', 'State', 'Public', 'Atmospheric', 'Boulder', 'Denver', or nearby spaces/digits only within such a frame. The bare generic word outside a Colorado frame is not reliable.

negative.name: Other-jurisdiction administrative/contact/citation identifier strings
negative.description: Negative on contact, citation, or grant strings tied to another jurisdiction in the prefix: North Dakota '(701) 328-1504' or a 701 phone in Game and Fish CWD material, N.D.C.C. '§ 28-33-02' with hyphens and digits, Nevada/Utah 775/435 phone strings, or Qinghai grant 'No. 11761056' with parentheses and digits. The cue is the other-jurisdiction administrative/identifier frame, often involving punctuation and digits; generic numbers, punctuation, or a non-Colorado place name alone are not reliable negatives.

negative.name: Other-jurisdiction legal/administrative boilerplate
negative.description: Negative on legal or administrative boilerplate for another jurisdiction: North Dakota Department of Agriculture/IPM address-phone block, North Dakota Game and Fish CWD contact, N.D.C.C. citations, and New Mexico or Qinghai grant/address material. Purely generic legal prose without a jurisdiction cue is weak or near zero. This rule does not suppress ordinary discussion of other states or regions, which can be positive or weak; it targets formatted other-jurisdiction administrative and legal identifiers.

output.what_would_change_my_mind: I would restore a non-Colorado place-name negative rule if many non-Colorado place contexts, including Bolivia, Nepal, Texas, Utah, and New Mexico, were consistently strongly negative rather than positive or weak. I would withdraw Colorado specificity if explicit Colorado names in the causal prefix were often weak or negative without an intervening factor. I would revise the administrative-negative rules if 701/775/435, N.D.C.C., or Qinghai grant strings were often strong positive. I would add a new positive rule if strong non-Colorado positives clustered around a nameable recurring expression; currently they remain unresolved. Tiny near-zero sign flips alone should not overturn the supported patterns.
